summary: Describes an optional feature for active measurement protocols, such as TWAMP, that lets them use the IEEE 1588v2 Precision Time Protocol timestamp format instead of the NTP format.

eli5.summary: Two clocks can write the time in two styles. This lets a measuring tool use the other style.

questions: how does twamp negotiate timestamp format
ntp vs ptp timestamp in twamp
subtitle: An optional way for TWAMP and OWAMP test packets to carry the more precise IEEE 1588 (PTP) timestamp instead of an NTP one.

tldr.problem: OWAMP and TWAMP test packets can only carry NTP-format timestamps, which come from clocks that are often accurate only to milliseconds and that must be converted from PTP in the data plane.
tldr.mechanism: One new bit in the Modes field lets the two ends agree on a PTPv2 timestamp format during connection setup, and the Z bit in the Error Estimate tells the receiver which format each packet uses.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints with PTP clocks can use them directly and stay compatible with nodes that only know NTP. It is an OPTIONAL feature on the Standards Track.

facts.label: Typical NTP accuracy over the Internet

today: RFC 8186 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Another Timestamp Format
sections.content:
The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP, RFC 4656) allows only the NTP format of a timestamp in its test protocol. The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) reuses the OWAMP-Test packet format and adds a reflected test packet. Timestamps in both directions are expected to follow the 64-bit NTP format.

The RFC points out two problems. NTP over the Internet typically gives clock accuracy within 5 ms to 100 ms, and it synchronizes clocks on the control plane, not the data plane, so queuing delays inside a node hurt data-plane accuracy. In contrast, the Precision Time Protocol (PTP, IEEE 1588v2) allows sub-microsecond accuracy and is supported in many fast-forwarding engines.

There is also a hardware argument: if the clock is PTP, test timestamps must be converted to NTP, which costs scarce resources such as microcode or extra processing elements. Using the PTP format directly simplifies the data plane.
sections.eli5: An old clock that is only right to within a blink is being replaced by a stopwatch that is right to the tiny fraction of a second. Using the stopwatch directly saves you from converting its numbers into the old clock's style.

sections.title: Negotiating the Format in the Modes Field
sections.content:
Connection setup in OWAMP and TWAMP already uses the Modes field to select capabilities, and that field has been used as an extension mechanism. This document takes one bit position in it, the PTPv2 Timestamp flag, so the Server and Control-Client can agree which timestamp format may be used in test sessions on that control connection.

An endpoint that supports the extension MUST be able to interpret both the NTP and the PTPv2 formats. An endpoint that does not support it leaves the flag at 0, because that bit sits in the Must Be Zero field. A flag value of 0 means the advertising node can use and interpret only NTP.

Implementations MAY offer a configuration knob that bypasses negotiation and uses locally configured values instead.

Backwards compatibility is an explicit goal: nodes that do not know this extension keep working with NTP timestamps.
sections.eli5: Before a game, both players say which scoreboard they can read. If one player only reads the old scoreboard, everyone uses the old one.

sections.title: OWAMP and TWAMP Setup Rules
sections.content:
In OWAMP the Session-Receiver interprets the timestamps, so the Server uses the flag in the Server Greeting to say whether the Session-Receiver can read PTPv2. If the Control-Client sees 0, the Session-Sender MUST use NTP and the Control-Client SHOULD set the flag to 0 in the Set-Up-Response. If the Session-Sender cannot use NTP, the Control-Client SHOULD close the TCP connection of the OWAMP-Control session. If the greeting has 1 and the Session-Sender can produce PTPv2, the Control-Client MUST set the flag to 1 and the Session-Sender MUST use PTPv2. When Fetch-Session commands are used, the choice is a local decision for both ends.

In TWAMP the Session-Sender interprets the timestamps, so the Server advertises what the Session-Reflector can use. The Server MUST set the flag to 1 in its greeting if the Session-Reflector can set PTPv2 timestamps, and otherwise MUST set it to 0. The Control-Client MUST set the flag to 1 in the Set-Up-Response if the Server advertised that ability, and otherwise MUST set it to 0. If the Set-Up-Response carries 0, the Session-Reflector MUST use NTP, and if it cannot, the Server MUST close the TCP connection of the TWAMP-Control session. The Session-Sender's own choice of format is a local decision.
sections.eli5: The side that reads the results says which styles it understands, and the side that writes the numbers picks one that both can handle. If there is no match, they hang up instead of guessing.

sections.title: Marking the Format in Test Packets
sections.content:
Test participants need to say which format a given timestamp uses. The Error Estimate of RFC 4656 already has a Z field, and this document extends the Error Estimate so it also indicates the format of the collected timestamp, alongside the error and synchronization estimate. The Z bit (the field between S and Scale) is now called the Timestamp format and MUST be set to 0 for the NTP 64-bit format or 1 for the PTPv2-truncated format.

Because of this, the Sender Error Estimate (TWAMP) or Send Error Estimate (OWAMP) and the Receive Error Estimate SHOULD NOT be ignored and MUST be used when calculating delay and delay-variation metrics from the collected timestamps.

For TWAMP Light mode, the document does not say how the Session-Sender and Session-Reflector learn the format. It assumes, for example, that configuration could direct them to use the format their capabilities and the rules of the TWAMP setup allow.
sections.eli5: Each measurement note gets a tiny tag saying which clock style it was written in, so the reader never mixes them up.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered a new entry in the TWAMP-Modes registry (defined in RFC 5618): bit position 9, named PTPv2 Timestamp Capability, with semantics given in Section 2 of this document.
sections.eli5: The official list of switches got one new switch, number 9, that means 'I can read the new clock style'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that using a particular timestamp format in a test session does not appear to add any security threat to hosts that communicate with OWAMP or TWAMP as defined in RFC 4656 and RFC 5357. The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks still apply, and readers are pointed to the security sections of those two RFCs.
sections.eli5: Writing the time in a different style does not open any new doors for troublemakers, but the old safety rules for measuring still apply.
